# Sharp quantitative vertex averaging and general facet-roof extraction

This is an ordinary simplex functional theorem. It supplies no mixed
integer center or global allocation argument by itself.

Let d>=2, let F={x_i>=0, sum_i x_i=1} have d barycentric coordinates,
let mu be its normalized (d-1)-dimensional volume, and let
g=(1/d,...,1/d). For Z uniform on F and an independent uniform vertex
label I, write Y_b=(1-b)Z+b e_I. For 0<=b<=1/d define

    a=1-db, h=1-b,
    c_d(b)=[a-a^d/h^(d-1)]/(d-1)^2.                 (1)

For every continuous concave psi on F,

    E psi(Y_b)-E psi(Z)
       >=c_d(b)[psi(g)-E psi(Z)].                  (2)

This constant is exact. It is positive for 0<b<1/d, and equality
holds for psi(x)=min_i x_i. In particular, at b=1/(d+1),

    c_d=[1-d^(1-d)]/[(d-1)^2(d+1)].                (3)

The only nontrivial dependency is the independently proved constructive
critical convex-order theorem in
`candidate c6aadce19d219a98`: in k>=2
coordinates, Y_s is dominated in convex order by uniform volume for
0<=s<=1/k. Its proof uses the minimum-coordinate partition and an
explicit elementary merging martingale, and does not use (2), ordinary
Grunbaum stability, or OC. In one coordinate the simplex is a point.

## 1. Minimum-coordinate disintegration at every subcritical step

Take 0<b<1/d first. The density of Y_b relative to mu is

    N_b(y)/[d h^(d-1)],  N_b(y)=#{i:y_i>=b}.        (4)

The finitely many tied-minimum hyperplanes are null. By permutation
symmetry the minimum label L has uniform law. Conditional on L=i,
write

    t=d y_i,  y_i=t/d,
    y_j=t/d+(1-t)w_j  (j!=i), sum_(j!=i) w_j=1.   (5)

For uniform volume on this minimum cell, t and w are independent:

    p(t)=(d-1)(1-t)^(d-2), 0<t<1,

and w is uniform on the opposite (d-2)-simplex. This follows from
the affine barycentrics of conv(g,{e_j:j!=i}), whose slice Jacobian
is (1-t)^(d-2). Since both laws give the cell mass1/d, (4) is also
the conditional density relative to this uniform product law.

Put theta=db. If t<theta, the minimum coordinate is below b and

    y_j>=b iff w_j>=s(t),
    s(t)=(b-t/d)/(1-t),  0<=s(t)<=b.               (6)

The conditional w law is the vertex-averaging law in d-1 coordinates
at step s(t). Indeed its density is proportional to the number of
coordinates at least s(t), and the normalizing factor is exactly
(d-1)(1-s(t))^(d-2). When d=2 the opposite simplex is a point and
this assertion simply means that point law. When t>theta, every
coordinate is above b, so the conditional w law is uniform instead.

The marginal density q of t is therefore

    q(t)/p(t)
      =(d-1)/(d h^(d-1))
          *[(h-((d-1)/d)t)/(1-t)]^(d-2), t<theta,
      =h^(-(d-1)),                              t>theta. (7)

This integrates to one because it was obtained by marginalizing (4).
The ratio is nondecreasing in t. On the first interval the expression
inside the power has derivative

    (1/d-b)/(1-t)^2>=0.

At theta it jumps upward from (d-1)/(d h^(d-1)) to h^(-(d-1));
on the second interval it is constant. For d=2 the first interval
is constant, with the same upward jump. Values at the single dividing
point have no effect on the law.

The critical theorem applies to (6), since for d>=3,
s(t)<=b<1/d<1/(d-1). Thus for any convex function f on F,
conditional on i,t its expectation under the Y_b law is at most
its expectation with w replaced by a uniform point on the opposite
facet. This replacement keeps i and t fixed. It does not replace
Y_b itself by a uniform point in F.

## 2. A one-dimensional covariance estimate on every radial ray

Let f be continuous, convex, nonnegative on F, with f(g)=0. Put
R=1-t. Let p_R and q_R be the densities obtained from p and q.
Equation (7) says Q(R)=q_R(R)/p_R(R) is nonincreasing in R.
For each fixed boundary point w on an opposite facet, define

    F_w(r)=f(g+r(w-g)), 0<=r<=1.

Convexity and F_w(0)=0 imply that F_w(r)/r is nondecreasing for
r>0: apply convexity to r=(r/s)s+(1-r/s)0 when r<s. It is
nonnegative and bounded above by F_w(1).

Under the probability law with density r p_R(r)/E_p R, an increasing
function and a decreasing function have nonpositive covariance.
For completeness, if U,V are independent with this law, the product

    [F_w(U)/U-F_w(V)/V][Q(U)-Q(V)]

is nonpositive pointwise. Integrating and expanding gives precisely
the covariance assertion. All factors are bounded here. Consequently

    E_q F_w(R)
        <=[E_q R/E_p R] E_p F_w(R).                (8)

Use the conditional convex-order bound of Section1 first, then (8)
for each i,w, and finally integrate over their uniform laws. This gives

    E f(Y_b)<=[E_q R/E_p R] E f(Z).                (9)

No differentiability or strict convexity of f is needed. The argument
also controls functions with curvature concentrated close to a facet
or vertex; it does not appeal to compactness of normalized functions.

## 3. Exact radial moments and the sharp constant

For the original independent construction Y_b, translation of the
constrained simplex coordinates gives

    P(min_i Y_(b,i)>=u)
      =[1-(d-1)u/h]^(d-1), 0<=u<=b,
      =[(1-du)/h]^(d-1),   b<=u<=1/d,
      =0,                 u>1/d.                 (10)

In the first interval only the d-1 unraised coordinates are constrained;
in the second all d coordinates are constrained. The first expression
remains nonnegative because b<=1/d. Direct integration gives

    E min_i Y_(b,i)
      =h/[d(d-1)]-a^d/[d^2(d-1)h^(d-1)].          (11)

For uniform Z, E min_i Z_i=1/d^2 and E_p R=(d-1)/d. As t=d min Y,

    1-E_q R/E_p R
      =[d^2 E min_i Y_(b,i)-1]/(d-1)
      =[a-a^d/h^(d-1)]/(d-1)^2=c_d(b).            (12)

A continuous concave function psi has a supporting affine majorant
ell at the relative interior point g, with ell(g)=psi(g). This is
the supporting-hyperplane theorem for its convex hypograph; alternatively
separate that hypograph from points directly above (g,psi(g)) and
take a convergent normalized separating normal. Interior local boundedness
ensures a nonvertical support and hence a finite affine majorant.
The function f=ell-psi is convex, nonnegative and vanishes at g.
Both Z and Y_b have mean g, so (9)-(12) give (2).

The endpoint b=0 is the identity. At b=1/d, c_d(b)=0 and the critical
convex-order theorem proves (2); it is also the limit of this proof.
There is no undefined zero power in (1) since d>=2.

To verify sharpness, take psi=min_i x_i and ell=1/d. On every ray
from g to a boundary facet, f=R/d. Therefore (8) is an equality,
and the conditional facet replacement also preserves f exactly:
the minimum coordinate remains t/d. Equivalently, (11) directly gives
equality in (2). Since psi(g)-E psi(Z)=(d-1)/d^2>0, no larger
coefficient is possible. Substitution b=1/(d+1) gives (3).

## 4. All concave functions on a simplex facet

Now let d also be the dimension of an ordinary simplex T in R^d,
with standard volume V=1/d!, and let its top facet have the above
d barycentric coordinates. Set m=d+1, h=d/m, Gamma=h^d and

    N(s)=#{i:s_i>=1/m},
    E_d(psi)=int_F [N(s)-m Gamma] psi(s) dmu(s).

The exact identity d h^(d-1)=m Gamma and the density formula imply

    E_d(psi)=m Gamma[E psi(Y_(1/m))-E psi(Z)].       (13)

For every continuous concave psi, its supporting affine majorant ell
at the facet centroid thus satisfies the sharp estimate

    int_F (ell-psi) dmu
      =psi(g)-int_F psi dmu
      <=E_d(psi)/(m Gamma c_d).                    (14)

In particular E_d(psi)>=0, with equality only for affine psi. To
justify the last claim, ell-psi is nonnegative and continuous, and
zero integral forces it to vanish everywhere on F. The exact constant
in (14) is attained by psi=min_i s_i. This controls arbitrary concave
facet functions, with no restriction to a single coordinate.

## 5. Actual fixed-roof bodies and an enclosing simplex

Let psi>=0 be a fixed continuous concave function on the standard
(d-1)-simplex Z={z_j>=0,sum z_j<=1}. In coordinates (z,r), put

    K_epsilon={z in Z: sum z_j-1<=r<=epsilon psi(z)}.

The affine map (z,r)->(z,1-sum z_j+r) has determinant one and
identifies K_0 with T. For epsilon>0 this is a convex body containing
T, with exact volume V+epsilon d V int psi. Write the affine majorant
in (14) as ell(z)=A+sum B_j z_j. It is nonnegative on Z. Dropping
the base restriction sum z_j<=1 and using the same lower and upper
planes defines an enclosing simplex S_epsilon; in the coordinates
q=r-sum z_j+1 its inequalities are

    q>=0, z_j>=0,
    q+sum_j(1-epsilon B_j)z_j<=1+epsilon A.

For sufficiently small epsilon all coefficients and the right side
are positive. It contains K_epsilon and has exact volume

    |S_epsilon|=V(1+epsilon A)^d
                         /product_j(1-epsilon B_j). (15)

Thus its relative missing volume satisfies

    1-|K_epsilon|/|S_epsilon|
      =epsilon d int(ell-psi)+O_psi(epsilon^2).      (16)

The already audited ordinary weak-added-law maximum-depth variation
in `candidate 7ff8cebaefda7361`
gives, for this FIXED roof,

    D(K_epsilon)=Gamma+epsilon(d/m)E_d(psi)+o_psi(epsilon). (17)

Here D is normalized maximum halfspace depth. For clarity, the added
measure divided by epsilon converges to psi times facet coordinate
volume. Its canonical centroid-hyperplane boundaries are null on the
facet, and its total mass is d V int psi. The unnormalized maximum
variation is the average of its m canonical cap masses. Subtracting
the normalization term gives exactly (17). The all-normal proof and
localization are the audited weak-added-law theorem; no merely fixed
canonical-normal minimization is assumed.

For every fixed nonaffine psi, (14)-(17) imply

    liminf_(epsilon->0)
      [D(K_epsilon)-Gamma]/[1-|K_epsilon|/|S_epsilon|]
                                             >=Gamma c_d. (18)

The denominator has positive linear coefficient in this case. Nested
uniform total variation and cap distance are at most that missing
fraction. No uniform relative remainder for varying roofs is asserted.
If psi is affine, the linear deficit and the linear missing-volume
term both vanish; (18) is not inferred from a zero-over-zero expansion.
The exact containing simplex (15) still exists in that case.
